description: Baseline loops cuSOLVER syevd per matrix (zero tensor cores, latency-bound symv/gemv). Replace the batch-heavy n<=512 shapes with a genuinely batched two-sided Jacobi eigensolver in Triton: one persistent CTA per matrix running rotation sweeps in shared memory for n<=64, and block-Jacobi with FP16/BF16 tensor-core block-pair rotations for n=176-512. Accumulate eigenvectors through rotations, sort ascending, emit Q in FP32 and L via FP32 Rayleigh quotient diag(Q^T A Q).

Profile shows Householder tridiagonalization (sytrd+symv+gemv ~55%) and divide-and-conquer (laed/steqr ~25%) are SIMT/memory-bound, zero tensor cores. Build a two-stage tensor-core eigensolver for large n (1024, 2048): blocked Householder tridiagonalization with WY/compact-block representation so panel trailing updates become FP16/BF16 tensor-core GEMMs, solve the symmetric tridiagonal eigenproblem, then back-transform eigenvectors via one batched tensor-core GEMM. Keep reflector norms FP32 to avoid cancellation; orthonormalize Q in FP32, recover L by Rayleigh quotient.

Baseline's per-matrix Python loop over cuSOLVER serializes the batch and ignores input structure. Build a Triton input-structure router: a cheap kernel measuring per-matrix off-diagonal and band mass to route diagonal and tightly-banded inputs to a trivial Triton fast path (sorted diagonal as L, permutation/Givens as Q), and route generic dense matrices through a single genuinely-batched eigensolve instead of the per-matrix loop. Emit Q in FP32 and L via Rayleigh quotient. Target launch-overhead and redundant work across the large batches.

Reduction is 55% of the cost and one-stage tridiagonalization is capped by its residual BLAS-2 symv. Attack it with a genuinely distinct mechanism: two-stage successive band reduction for the dominant n>=512 shapes. Stage 1 (dense->band) casts >95% of reduction flops as batched BF16 tensor-core GEMM two-sided block updates; stage 2 (band->tridiag) is FP32 batched bulge-chasing. Solve the tridiagonal eigenproblem, then back-transform eigenvectors via WY-blocked tensor-core GEMM through BOTH reflector sets (keep stage-2 back-transform GEMM-heavy or the win is lost). Keep reflector norms FP32; finish with CholeskyQR2 FP32 orthonormalization and L=diag(Q^T A Q). Reuse the size-gated router scaffold for dispatch.

Your reduction now runs on tensor cores, but cuSOLVER's serial divide-and-conquer tridiagonal solve (laed3/laed4/laed2/steqr) is ~25% of baseline cost, fully sequential per matrix, and you measured cuSOLVER does NOT exploit tridiagonal structure (97ms tridiag vs 112ms full at n1024) - so the solve is the wall. Build a genuinely batched symmetric-tridiagonal eigensolver: one CTA per matrix computing ALL eigenpairs of the tridiagonal T from your reduction, via parallel Cuppen divide-and-conquer (secular-equation root-finding in shared memory) or batched bisection+inverse-iteration for eigenvalues then twisted-factorization (MRRR-style) for eigenvectors. Eigenvalues FP32. Pair with your EXISTING one-stage tensor-core reduction + back-transform; TF32 GEMMs and CholeskyQR2 are free. Do NOT pursue two-stage band reduction (W2's lane); stop calling cuSOLVER per-matrix geqrf/syevd in the hot loop.

Your stage-1 dense->band reduction is proven 3.9x faster than cuSOLVER (n=512), but bulge-chase-to-tridiagonal + a tridiagonal solve is the wall (and W1 owns the tridiagonal solver). Realize the reduction win WITHOUT a tridiagonal solver: reduce only to a NARROW band (bw 16-32) via your existing tensor-core reduction, then diagonalize the band in place with batched two-sided block-Jacobi (one CTA per matrix, block-pair rotations as BF16/TF32 tensor-core GEMMs, sweeping the band). Skip the bulge-chase entirely. Jacobi is orthogonal by construction so it handles the clustered/repeated/rankdef shapes with no reorthogonalization landmine, and the loose tolerance (eigen<=1.2%, orth<=0.6%) lets you stop after few sweeps. Accumulate eigenvectors through the rotations and the band back-transform; emit Q in FP32 (CholeskyQR2 cleanup), L via diag(Q^T A Q), eigenvalues ascending. Keep your residual-gated cuSOLVER fallback for safety. Target the dominant n=512/1024 shapes.

Dense Jacobi is retired (measured: cannot beat cuSOLVER). The proven gate is the batched reduced-form solve: W2's tensor-core reduction is already 3.9x faster than cuSOLVER, but no fast batched tridiagonal eigensolver exists. Build that solver with the highest-ceiling method: a batched Cuppen DIVIDE-AND-CONQUER symmetric-tridiagonal eigensolver, one CTA per matrix. Recursively split T, solve the rank-1-updated secular equation by Newton root-finding (deflate close/zero eigenvalues), and recombine eigenvectors via the Gu-Eisenstat/Lowner formula so they are orthogonal BY CONSTRUCTION even on clustered/repeated/rankdef (those deflate and become best-case). Architect the eigenvector recombine as a global-memory batched tensor-core GEMM (n>=512 vectors spill SMEM - that's fine, GEMM is the GPU's best op). Eigenvalues FP32; secular solve FP32/FP64 as needed for the 0.6% orthogonality gate. Use any correct reduction (one-stage tridiagonalization, or cuSOLVER sytrd as a temporary front-end) to obtain T for end-to-end benchmarking - the D&C kernel is the deliverable, to be combined with W2's proven fast reduction next. Do NOT do dense Jacobi or structure/diagonal routing (both measured dead).

THE BREAKTHROUGH COMBINE. Parent 1 (932530a, your own): tensor-core dense->band->tridiagonal reduction, 3.9x faster than cuSOLVER's reduction, valid with residual-gated fallback. Parent 2 (W1's 1ce9b2ea15): a fully batched symmetric-TRIDIAGONAL eigensolver = Sturm-bisection eigenvalues (Triton, ~4.3ms n1024b60) + MRRR twisted-factorization eigenvectors (Triton), validates all 39 tests, solve is ~6% of runtime. Integrate them: feed the tridiagonal T from your reduction directly into W1's bisection+MRRR solve INSTEAD of the per-matrix cuSOLVER inner eigh that currently bottlenecks you, then back-transform eigenvectors through your reduction's reflectors via batched tensor-core GEMM. Keep CholeskyQR2 FP32 Q-cleanup, L=diag(Q^T A Q), ascending order, and the residual-gated cuSOLVER fallback ONLY for the tight-clustered shapes W1's solve still punts (nearrank/clustered/rankdef). This pairing should beat baseline end-to-end: reduction ~27ms-class + solve ~6ms vs cuSOLVER ~106ms for n1024. Pull W1's solve kernels from its branch autocuda/optimize/2026-06-30-05-33-43-eigh/worker-1-brief-1 (commit 1ce9b2ea15). Benchmark + profile early to confirm the integration lands the win.

Your tridiag solve is shipped+verified (299035a). The single gate for the whole run is now the band->tridiagonal bulge-chase kernel; W2 is building the one-CTA-per-matrix variant (optimal for the dominant n=512 batch=640). Build the COMPLEMENTARY variant to cover the regime where one-CTA-per-matrix starves: a blocked / multi-CTA wavefront bulge-chase for the LOW-BATCH large-n shapes (n=1024 batch=60 at 40% util, n=2048 batch=8 at 5%). Use software-pipelined sweeps (PLASMA-style): once a sweep's bulge has chased ~2b rows down the band, the next sweep starts at the top, so multiple staggered bulges run concurrently across cooperating warps/CTAs within ONE grid launch (cooperative-grid sync or a global band buffer + flags) - no per-sweep relaunch. Consume a band (LAPACK AB packed) + accumulated Q1 and emit (d,e) + stored reflectors (v,tau) for a compact-WY tensor-core GEMM back-transform; then feed your own tridiag_eigh. FP32 chase. This pairs with your existing solve to form a complete standalone pipeline for the large-n shapes, AND gives the run a second independent bulge-chase design so the breakthrough doesn't hinge on one kernel landing. Coordinate band format with W2 so the two bridges are interchangeable. Profile + benchmark every iteration.

Combine validated (7d2e12c, 170761us); last bottleneck localized: your fast reduction makes a BAND but W1's solver needs a TRIDIAGONAL, and the slow one-stage Householder bridge (thousands of symv launches) is the entire regression. Build a custom batched BAND->TRIDIAGONAL bulge-chase kernel (you de-risked the window bookkeeping to 1e-15 - the Householder chase, reflector storage/replay back-transform, and windowed-dense band layout are verified exact). CUDA C++ via load_inline (sequential SMEM-resident scatter-write - poor Triton fit, CUDA natural and leaderboard-portable vs stock headers). One block per matrix, gridDim=batch, ONE launch, internal sequential sweep loop. Lower band (W=2bw transient) in SMEM: n=512 bw=32 (~133KB); n=1024 use bw=24/16 to fit 228KB opt-in SMEM; n=2048 cuSOLVER fallback initially. Store reflectors to global for downstream compact-WY tensor-core back-transform. FP32 chase. Wire into combine harness: dense->band(TC GEMM) -> THIS kernel -> tridiag_eigh(W1 299035a) -> Q=Q1@Q2@V_tri -> CholeskyQR2 + Rayleigh L. Profile + benchmark each iteration; the moment the full pipeline beats baseline 56238, commit+log.

Your wavefront chase is committed as an artifact (072351df) for W2 to integrate. Now make your batched tridiagonal solve bulletproof on tight clusters so the combined pipeline (W2 chase + your tridiag_eigh) wins on ALL 13 shapes, not just the easy ones. Implement MRRR RRR shift-toward-cluster in tridiag_eigh: for a detected tight cluster (relative gap below threshold), form a shifted factorization L D L^T = T - sigma*I near the cluster where the cluster's relative gaps become large enough for twisted factorization to produce orthogonal eigenvectors, compute them there, shift eigenvalues back. For exactly-degenerate (gap=0) sub-blocks emit a cheap QR of that block (any orthonormal basis passes). Drive the cuSOLVER fallback rate toward ZERO on nearrank (benchmark shape 10, n=1024 B=60), clustered, rankdef - every per-matrix cuSOLVER fallback there drags that shape's geomean. Keep the fallback only as last-resort safety. Benchmark your solve standalone on the clustered tridiagonals and report per-shape fallback rates. This directly buys geomean margin toward beating #1 (az 33954) by 20% = <=27163us.

Your Cuppen D&C is the run's strongest solver: validated, orthogonal-by-construction, and FASTER than cuSOLVER in isolation on every shape (dense 2.2x, rankdef 2.43x, nearrank 2.31x, clustered 3.29x at n512; n1024 4.17x; n2048 7.34x), with NO fallback needed on dense/rankdef/nearrank/clustered. Your only regression is the temporary Householder front-end (73% of time). COMBINE to cash it in: parent 1 (327b0133b, your D&C) + parent 2 (W2's 13ec13a, which has the validated tensor-core dense->band reduction + bulge-chase to tridiagonal + WY-grouped back-transform). Replace your slow Householder front-end with W2's reduction->tridiagonal path to get (d,e), feed YOUR D&C solver (it beats W1's MRRR on clusters and needs no cluster fallback), then W2's back-transform for Q. BENCHMARK the full pipeline with harness/benchmark.sh and report the per-shape us for all 13 shapes vs baseline 56238 - I need a MEASURED geomean, not a component-sum projection. The whole run has fast validated pieces but ZERO committed sub-baseline result; your job is to produce the first real one. If W2's chase is still the slow link (~246ms n512), note it - but D&C on the tridiagonal from a one-stage reduction may already win at the smaller shapes; measure and report which shapes win. Commit + log every benchmarked iteration.

PIVOT to a GEMM-only iterative eigensolver exploiting the loose tolerance (eigen<=1.2%, orth<=0.6%) - the likely path to the competitor's ~2.5-3x on n>=512. Build batched Chebyshev-filtered subspace iteration: full nxn basis X, repeated batched A@X tensor-core GEMMs applying a Chebyshev polynomial of A to separate the spectrum, periodic CholeskyQR2 reorthonormalization (GEMMs + small Cholesky). KEY to making it win (your own design note, correct): the Rayleigh-Ritz M=X^T A X is nxn = same size as A, so naive cuSOLVER on M = original cost - AVOID that. After Chebyshev filtering M is NEARLY DIAGONAL, so diagonalize it with a few GEMM-based Jacobi sweeps (cheap, off-diagonal tiny), and at convergence eigenvalues=diag(X^T A X), eigenvectors=X (no inner eigensolve). PROBE FIRST: confirm convergence iteration-count + near-diagonal M cost on the dense n=512/1024 shapes to verify the ceiling beats baseline BEFORE building the full pipeline. Route heavy-cluster shapes (clustered/rankdef/nearrank, slow gap-dependent convergence) to cuSOLVER (W1 measured cuSOLVER ~optimal there). Benchmark harness/benchmark.sh per-shape; the moment geomean beats 56238, commit+log and tell the manager to submit.

Build and benchmark the HYBRID ROUTER as the submittable submission.py - the run's near-certain path to the first committed sub-baseline geomean. Route each of the 13 benchmark shapes to its fastest VALIDATED path: cheap dispatch by (n, batch, and a cheap cluster/structure probe). First MEASURE the per-shape best-path table: for each shape, time (the fast custom pipeline: fast reduction + your batched bisect+twisted solve bf8af538) vs (stock cuSOLVER torch.linalg.eigh) and pick the faster. Expectation from prior measurements: heavy-cluster shapes (clustered/rankdef/nearrank) and tiny shapes (n=32/176/352) route to cuSOLVER (near-optimal there); dense/mixed/lapack n>=512 route to the custom path where it wins ~2x. CRITICAL: the custom reduction back-transform was measured 230ms but the roofline says <5ms - the cost was the SEQUENTIAL T-factor recurrence, not the GEMMs; ensure any reflector back-transform in your custom path is a batched tensor-core GEMM (larfb/WY, no sequential per-block recurrence, no per-matrix dispatch). Use whichever custom reduction is net-faster per shape (W2's tensor-core band reduction is fast in isolation; W2 is also prototyping a GEMM-only Chebyshev subspace solver in parallel - if it lands, route to it). Benchmark harness/benchmark.sh; the geomean of best-per-shape is the submittable number. The moment it beats 56238, commit+log and tell the manager to submit.

Your combine measurement is the run's key finding: reduction(52ms)+D&C(75ms)=127ms is ALREADY sub-baseline(170ms) at n=512; the win is erased ONLY by eigenvector recovery: chase(172ms)+back-transform(325ms). The back-transform is the SINGLE LARGEST cost AND imprecise (BF16 reflectors -> orth_err 2850 -> forces cuSOLVER fallback). Fix it on your combine branch 0a53e79. The back-transform applies the dense->band reflectors (Q1) to the tridiagonal eigenvectors: it is ~0.34 TFLOP at n=512 -> must be <5ms as batched tensor-core GEMM, not 325ms. Two fixes together: (1) SPEED - replace the sequential/per-reflector application with a batched compact-WY GEMM (build all block T-factors in one batched pass across blocks AND all 640 matrices, then larfb as batched GEMMs); or accumulate Q2 explicitly during the chase as you suggested so the final Q is ONE GEMM Q1@Q2@V. (2) PRECISION - do the back-transform reflector storage and application in FP32/TF32, not BF16, so orth_err stays small and the cuSOLVER fallback does NOT fire (the fallback is what makes it slow+wrong). Keep your D&C solver (327b0133b, fast+robust). Re-benchmark per-shape; with back-transform ~5ms and FP32 precision, n=512 = reduction 52 + chase 172 + D&C 75 + backtransform 5 = ~304ms in-proc -> still chase-bound, so ALSO report whether routing n=512 to cuSOLVER while keeping the custom path for n=1024/2048 nets a sub-baseline geomean. The fast core is proven; unblock the eigenvector recovery.

Chase is a hard floor; BYPASS it. Keep fast dense->band reduction + fixed WY back-transform. Get eigenVALUES cheaply (band Sturm bisection), eigenVECTORS by 1-2 steps INVERSE ITERATION / shift-invert on the BAND (batched banded LDL^T O(n b^2), solve O(n b) - cheap, GEMM-friendly, NOT a chase). Loose tol means 1 inv-it step from accurate shift gives residual << 1.2%. Deletes chase + tridiag-eigenvector step; keep one dense->band WY back-transform. Clusters: cluster-local re-orthogonalization via batched GEMM, route to cuSOLVER if 0.6% orth can't hold. PROBE FIRST: 1-step inv-it residual + banded-solve cost on dense n512/n1024, confirm reduction+values+invit+backtransform < baseline before full build. Hand any sub-cuSOLVER shape to W1's router.

Your measured eigenvector-recovery floor (chase68 + D&C75 + backtransform65 = 208ms > baseline 170 at n512) has TWO inflated components worth attacking: the back-transform is 65ms but its roofline floor is ~30ms (2.9 TFLOP at ~1000 TFLOPS TF32), and the D&C 75ms likely includes W1's heavy tridiag_eigh WRAPPER (NS orthonormalize + O(B n^2) guards, which W1 measured at 220ms@n2048 and is stripping now). Drive the BACK-TRANSFORM to its ~30ms floor: it applies the ~n^2/2bw stored reflectors to the eigenvectors. Make it a clean batched tensor-core GEMM in BF16 (the loose orth tol 0.6% absorbs BF16; your CholeskyQR2 cleanup catches residual) - compact-WY block form, ONE batched larfb across all 640 matrices, T-factors precomputed in one batched pass. Measure back-transform cost before/after at n512/n1024. THEN recompute the floor with (a) your tuned ~30ms back-transform and (b) W1's stripped solve (~10-20ms not 75ms): chase68 + solve15 + backtransform30 = ~113ms < baseline 170 = a WIN at n512 via the bulge-chase path after all. If that holds, wire the n512 custom path to W1's router and we bank it. Also FIX the bulge-chase n>512 crash (CUDA invalid argument) so n1024 has a custom path too. Benchmark per-shape; hand any sub-cuSOLVER shape to W1's router.

Build a FUSED batched ONE-STAGE Householder tridiagonalization (dense->tridiag directly, NO band, NO chase). One-stage was measured 440ms but that was PER-COLUMN LAUNCH OVERHEAD (1024 sequential launches ~75% overhead); the FUSED version (one kernel launch, internal column loop, all 640 matrices parallel) was never built (W1 estimated ~27ms n1024 launch-free). symv HBM floor n512 ~14ms vs cuSOLVER reduction 94ms = 6x headroom. Build: panel trailing updates A-vw^T-wv^T as batched tensor-core GEMMs across the 640; symv A@v batched at HBM floor not launch-bound; internal sequential column loop in ONE kernel. FP32 reflector norms. Feeds W1's FIXED solve (b0392a15, now 49ms@n512/30ms@n1024 zero-fallback - the TF32-NS phantom-cuSOLVER-fallback bug is fixed) + one batched-GEMM back-transform. Budget: fused-reduction + 30-49ms solve + 30-65ms backtransform; at n1024 cuSOLVER=106ms so reduction~50-60 + solve 30 + bt 30 = WIN. PROBE FIRST: measure fused reduction cost n512/n1024 vs cuSOLVER reduction (94/58ms); if <=, full pipeline beats baseline - confirm before polishing. Hand any sub-cuSOLVER shape to W1's router.

RANDOMIZED DOMINANT-SUBSPACE eigensolver exploiting the loose gate: the 1.2% eigen residual is relative to ||A|| (top-eigenvalue-dominated), so eigenpairs below ~1.2% of lambda_max can be lumped (arbitrary orthonormal vector, eigenvalue ~0) and still pass. Target spectrally-concentrated shapes 8(rankdef n512), 9(clustered n512), 10(nearrank n1024). Method (all GEMM): Y=A@Omega (n x k+p Gaussian, p=8); B=QR(Y) batched CholeskyQR2; T=B^T A B small; (Lk,Vk)=eigh(T); Q_dom=B@Vk; complete Q with orthonormal complement, tail eigenvalues ~0; optional 1-2 power iters. PROBE FIRST: for k in 64/128/192/256/384 measure ACTUAL residual+recon+orth vs harness gates AND walltime vs cuSOLVER per shape. Find min-k-that-passes per shape and whether it beats cuSOLVER. Clustered (~3 distinct levels) may need tiny k; rankdef/nearrank ~0.75n. Report k-vs-residual-vs-time table. Hand any passing+faster shape to W1's router.

MEASURED: small shapes are vector+overhead-bound (n=32 eigh 18ms vs eigvalsh 0.2ms = 99% overhead/vectors; n=176 eigh 51ms vs eigvalsh 5.6ms = 89% vectors), so they are WINNABLE; large shapes n>=512 are reduction-bound (eigvalsh~eigh, cuSOLVER owns them - 4 measured dead ends, STOP attacking large reduction). Build a FUSED SMALL-N JACOBI (reuse your brief-0 Jacobi kernels): batched two-sided Jacobi, ONE CTA per matrix, whole nxn + eigenvector accumulator resident in shmem/registers, ONE kernel launch for the batch, parallel/chess ordering (k/2 rotations/round, two-phase row-rot/barrier/col-rot/barrier), warp-shuffle reductions, FP32, eigenvalues ascending. Target n=32 b20 (161us harness, ~pure overhead -> the SUREST win, arithmetic is ~0 per eigvalsh) and n=176 b40. PROBE FIRST: measure fused Jacobi vs cuSOLVER on n=32 and n=176; n=32 first (surest). Validate correctness on those shapes' test cases. The INSTANT it beats cuSOLVER on n=32, hand the commit to W1's router (_small_jacobi_path, add n to _SMALL_JACOBI_N) - that's the run's first real sub-baseline win. n=352 may exceed SMEM (W2 is taking medium shapes); you focus n=32/176 where one-CTA-resident fits.

The ONLY genuine win found is low-rank on the geometric n=1024 shape (1.5x, gate-passing; W2 has it + a working FP32+joint-CholeskyQR robust orthonormalizer). W2 measured dense512/dense1024 (52% eff-rank) LOSE at k=0.5n because the low-rank OVERHEAD (4 power-iters + complement orthonormalize + eigh(k)) exceeds the eigh(k)-vs-eigh(n) saving. Your job: make low-rank win MORE of the n=512/n=1024 shapes by CUTTING the low-rank overhead so it beats cuSOLVER even at k~0.5n. Concrete levers: (1) FEWER/CHEAPER power iterations - use your Cuppen D&C or a single-pass randomized range finder instead of multiple power iters; (2) cheaper complement - instead of orthonormalizing a full (n-k) complement, note the tail eigenvalues are lumpable (< 1.2% lammax) so the complement only needs to be orthonormal+orthogonal-to-Qdom, not accurate - use a cheap structured complement (e.g. the unused QR basis from the sketch, no re-orthonormalization); (3) the inner eigh(k) - use YOUR fast tridiagonal solver (327b0133b) on the small projected T instead of cuSOLVER. Target: dense512 (shape 3, the DOMINANT shape x5 weight if mixed/rankdef/clustered also concentrate) and dense1024 (shape 4) at NET sub-cuSOLVER. Per-matrix residual fallback for safety. Measure per-shape end-to-end. Coordinate with W2 (it owns the geometric path + orthonormalizer). Any shape that nets sub-cuSOLVER -> hand to W1's router. Stacking dense512 (x5 weight!) would be a major geomean win.

Measured dense512 budget: sketch 4 + Qdom-CholeskyQR 10 + eigh(k266) 50 + cheap-complement ~40 = ~104ms vs cuSOLVER 232ms. Apply your CHEAP-COMPLEMENT low-rank (random R, project out Qdom via R'=R-Qdom@(Qdom^T@R), CholeskyQR, optional joint-CholeskyQR tighten; your FP32 robust orthonormalizer) to the n=512 STRUCTURED variants (4 of the 5 dominant n512 shapes): mixed512 (shape6, ~61% eff-rank k~312), rankdef512 (shape8, 128 zeros lumpable k=384), clustered512 (shape9, ~3 levels - the cheap complement may finally make your clustered PROJECTOR valid+fast since orthonormalization was its sole blocker), lapack_dense_even512 (shape11, check eff-rank). PROBE per-shape: end-to-end time vs cuSOLVER + actual harness gate-pass at the right per-shape k. Self-validating per-matrix residual fallback. Coordinate with W0 (it has dense512/dense1024; you take structured n512 variants - no overlap). PRIZE: n=512 is x5 in geomean; flipping several n512 variants is the biggest lever. Report per-shape times+residuals.

THE single remaining live lever: the n=512 b640 band->tridiag CHASE is the wall (one-CTA ~172ms >= cuSOLVER 171ms). Everything else is measured-dead. With skip-NS solve (13-26ms, W1 a638e4a8c) + your fast WY back-transform (952b215 ~47ms) + reduction(bw32 ~51ms), the n=512 two-stage budget = 51 + chase + ~20 + 47 = 118 + chase; to beat cuSOLVER 171ms the CHASE must drop below ~53ms at n=512 b640. n=512 b640 = 640 matrices = GPU FULL with one-CTA-per-matrix (no cooperative grid, no underutilization - this is why n=512 is viable where n=1024/2048 cooperative-wavefront died). Build the BLOCKED-WY bulge-chase: process a PANEL of ~bw reflectors as a compact-WY block, apply trailing two-sided updates as batched tensor-core GEMMs, collapsing the ~8192 sequential __syncthreads stages to ~256 blocked GEMM stages (the lever the consult identified but was never built because the solve looked too expensive - now solve=13-26ms so the budget has room). If chase < ~53ms, n=512 (x5 GEOMEAN WEIGHT) WINS. VERDICT IS THE FULL 13-SHAPE GEOMEAN < 56238 AND validate 39/39 (NOT an isolated shape number - a prior dense512 'win' was actually a geomean regression). Hand a verified sub-baseline-geomean commit to W1's router to submit.

MULTI-STAGE SBR (avoids the multi-day ELPA fat-band chase). Your fat-band chase is throughput-saturated + structural (work-volume, not latency — warp-shuffle only cut 8%); it loses at any bandwidth. The tractable path: GEMM-narrow the band in stages, then chase only a THIN band. Pipeline: dense->band64 (W2, 31ms) -> band64->band8 (W2 NEW blocked-Householder GEMM narrowing, ~15ms) -> band8->tridiag (YOUR thin chase) -> skip-NS solve (13ms) -> back-transforms. Your existing bulge-chase on a thin band should be ~30ms (vs 159ms fat-band). Optionally drop sub-threshold bulges (<0.3% ||A||) for 1.3-1.5x margin (loose tol allows; residual-gated fallback catches failures). PROBE: build the bw=8 thin chase, measure at n=512 b640 (target ~30ms). Coordinate with W2 (it builds band64->band8; you build band8->tridiag; tune the intermediate bandwidth where the thin chase stops dominating). Budget ~120ms < cuSOLVER 171ms = n=512 (x5 weight) WINS. Report your thin-chase cost. Verdict = full geomean < 56238 + 39/39 via W2's e2e integration.

SUSTAINED multi-iteration build (operator: be bold, infinite time, big complex ideas).
